claims.text: The target material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in the cast state.
Applying an oxidation-resistant coating will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The coating will preserve the alloy's useful mechanical performance.
A coating-alloy interface is the structural mediator of the intervention.
The oxidation-resistant coating will prevent or reduce oxygen diffusion into HfNbTaTiZr.
Reduced oxygen diffusion will reduce oxide-layer formation.
Reduced oxide-layer formation will improve resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
The coating may increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
The coating may increase elevated-temperature ductility.
Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr is the baseline for comparison.
The proposed comparison is relevant at 1000 °C.
The proposed comparison is conducted in an oxidizing atmosphere.
Several hours is the proposed oxidation-exposure duration.
Mechanical performance is to be evaluated in tension at strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^-2 s^-1.
The uncoated NbTaHfTiZr alloy has useful strength and ductility at normal temperature.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires improved oxidation resistance while merely preserving mechanical performance, and the predicted mechanical increase is only described as potential. The falsification rule nevertheless treats a lack of significant mechanical-performance improvement as falsifying, so a coating that improves oxidation resistance and retains unchanged mechanical properties could satisfy the hypothesis but fail its stated test.
